description_full: Ingram Micro Holding Corporation, through its subsidiaries, distributes information technology (IT) products, cloud, and other services in North America, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, the Asia-Pacific, and Latin America. The company offers client and endpoint solutions, including desktop personal computers, notebooks, tablets, printers, hard drives, motherboards, video cards, application software, peripherals, accessories, phones, tablets, smart and feature phones, mobile phone accessories, wearables, and mobility software for corporate and individual end users. It also provides enterprise-grade hardware and software products, such as servers, storage, networking, and hybrid and software-defined solutions, as well as cybersecurity, power, and cooling solutions; training, professional services, and related financing solutions; and data capture/point-of-sale, physical security, audio visual and digital signage, unified communications and collaboration, and smart office/home automation and artificial intelligence products. In addition, the company offers third-party cloud-based services and subscriptions, including business applications, security, communications and collaboration, cloud enablement solutions, and infrastructure-as-a-service, as well as IT asset disposition, reverse logistics, repair, and other related solutions. It serves value-added and corporate resellers, retailers, custom installers, systems integrators, mobile network operators, mobile virtual network operators, direct marketers, internet-based resellers, independent dealers, product category specialists, reseller purchasing associations, managed service providers, cloud services providers, PC assemblers, independent agents and dealers, IT and mobile device manufacturers, and other distributors. The company was founded in 1979 and is headquartered in Irvine, California.

financial_summary: Ingram Micro Holding Corporatio is a mid-cap technology business with a $6.5B market cap on $52.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 9% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 7% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $785M in free cash flow — roughly 1 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.79× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.2× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 2.9× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 1.2%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $1544.9M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake

Technology sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 7% over 3 months

Antitrust and platform-regulation risk — the larger the network effect, the larger the regulatory target on its back, and a single consent decree can reset the moat.
AI disruption of existing software moats — incumbents with durable margins face commoditisation as AI-native competitors replicate features at a fraction of the R&D cost.
Cybersecurity liability and talent cost inflation — a single breach can erase years of goodwill, and the war for engineering talent compresses margins even at scale.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 40% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 45% and a beta of 1.13, it moves roughly with the market.
About $43.7M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 2.0x its yearly average volume.
val: The stock trades 75% below its DCF fair value of $112, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 33%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $76.06 to $168 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 14.4 vs 27.4, EV/EBITDA 7.7 vs 17.1 and P/FCF 8.3 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 12.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 13 covering analysts target $32.85 on average, 16% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 8.9% annual cash-flow growth, 24pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 9% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.7%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.11).
It runs a 7% gross margin and converts 1% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.79x.
ROE of 8% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (5.0x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.2x net debt to EBITDA ($1.9B of cash against $3.2B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.9x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.2, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 9.5% over 3 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (0.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 9.5% on average.
Analysts expect 8.9% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.9%), and institutions hold 95%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (9 sales, net $1.5B sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.2% (1.2% in dividends).
Short interest is elevated at 21.0% of the float, 4.2 days to cover.
people: With about 22,200 employees, each generates about $2.4M of revenue, 6.4x the Technology median.
That works out to $35K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.6M (2x revenue per employee).
